title: A Continent of Nations
objective: After this level you can describe the variety of Native nations, languages and ways of life in North America before 1492.
summary: At European contact, North America north of Mexico spoke about 300 languages. Culture areas group its many ways of life, from Northwest Coast salmon to three sisters farms.

cards.headline: When Europeans arrived, North America spoke about 300 languages, not one.
cards.body: Each language came with its own people and way of life. Here’s how to picture that variety without memorizing a list.

cards.headline: More variety than Europe
cards.body: At European contact, North America north of Mexico had about 300 distinct languages. The linguist Edward Sapir found that the languages of California alone showed more variety than all of Europe’s. Picture a road trip up the California coast needing more phrasebooks than a grand tour of Europe.

cards.headline: Sorting a continent
cards.body: To make sense of so much variety, anthropologists group Native North America into culture areas: regions where similar ways of life occurred, such as the Northeast, the Plains, the Southwest and the Northwest Coast. Some peoples lived by hunting and gathering; others were farmers. A culture area is a map label, not a nation: each one held many different peoples.

items.label: Northwest Coast
points: Abundant salmon and other fish, sea mammals and shellfish
Large houses built of timber planks

items.label: Farming peoples
points: Corn, beans and squash planted together
The Iroquois and Cherokee called them the three sisters

cards.headline: Three crops, one team
cards.body: Why plant three crops in one field? In a three sisters field, corn stalks support the climbing beans, the beans add nitrogen to the soil, and the broad squash leaves shade out weeds and keep the soil moist. Each sister does a job for the others. It’s a garden with a group chat.

cards.headline: A continent of nations
learned: About 300 languages north of Mexico at contact
